regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 56.5","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks like a clean expansion — until you note that the FY estimate has been revised down to 7.1% YoY and core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY even as IIP capital goods surged 16.9% YoY. The divergence is structural: investment is accelerating while the goods economy (core sector, cement, steel) is not keeping pace. PMI Composite at 56.5 is services-led; if services credit at 28.3% YoY is funding consumption rather than productive capacity, the quality of this growth is thinner than the headline.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 6.09% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"CPI at 6.09% YoY — rising three consecutive months from 3.21% — has broken above the RBI's 6% tolerance ceiling, and the decomposition is uncomfortable: food at 8.94% YoY is the headline driver, but core CPI has also accelerated to 4.5% YoY. Fuel at 22.93% YoY, a 95th-percentile print, is the second-order threat: it feeds WPI at 9.92% YoY, compresses corporate margins, and eventually passes through to core with a two-quarter lag. The RBI's own inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY now looks like a forecast in need of revision.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.54% YoY; CD ratio 82%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.54% YoY — rising three consecutive months — against deposit growth at 16.86% YoY is a 268 bps divergence that has pushed the CD ratio to 82%, its 75th percentile. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% with credit accelerating, the eventual correction came through deposit rate wars, NIM compression, and macro-prudential tightening on risk weights. Services credit at 28.3% YoY (rising three months) is the fastest-growing segment — and the least collateralised. If deposit mobilisation doesn't catch up within two quarters, the RBI will act through the regulatory channel, not the rate channel.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the real rate is being eroded in real time: CPI at 6.09% YoY puts the real repo rate at negative 84 bps, the most accommodative it has been this cycle. The RBI's 'extended pause' is increasingly a fiction — with inflation above the tolerance band, the next move is more likely a hike than a cut, regardless of what the forward curve is pricing. For housing affordability, the average home loan rate at 7.35% p.a. already prices in tightening; for corporate capex IRRs, the question is whether capacity utilisation at 77.4% justifies new investment at these funding costs.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — both rising — confirm the investment upcycle is real, not budgetary. The 77.4% utilisation level is the threshold above which private capex historically accelerates in India; the last two cycles (FY08, FY12) saw private investment surge once utilisation crossed 78%. Iron ore at $161.91/t — nearly double the prior month's $90.67/t — signals construction and steel demand is pulling forward. The risk: if credit tightening arrives before utilisation crosses 80%, the private capex impulse stalls before it becomes self-sustaining.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹231290 cr/mo; PV 32.1% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,31,290 cr / month — a 90th-percentile print — is the broadest demand signal available, but the composition matters: a ₹43,165 cr jump in a single month warrants scrutiny on advance filings and year-end compliance effects before declaring a demand surge. Passenger vehicle sales at 32.1% YoY and two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY are the cleaner proxies — two-wheelers in particular signal rural and semi-urban demand recovery, which had been the weak link. Commercial vehicle sales at 37.6% YoY confirm freight demand is real. The inversion: housing credit is falling three consecutive months to 10.6% YoY even as vehicle credit runs at 18.8% YoY — consumers are buying cars, not homes.","badge_label":"Demand Surge","badge_type":"b-exp"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.54% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 16.86% YoY — a 268 bps divergence widening for three consecutive months (13.8→17.1→19.4→19.54% credit; 10.8→17.8→16.86% deposits). CD ratio at 82% credit ÷ deposits, up from 81% last month, now at 75th percentile of 10-year range. Services credit surging at 28.3% YoY (21.4→22.9→24.3→28.3%, three months rising), agriculture at 19.5% YoY (16.8→17→17.2→19.5%), while housing credit decelerating at 10.6% YoY (falling three months: 11.4→11.3→11.1→10.6%).","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% — they'll poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; NBFC credit growth already cooling to 15.4% YoY from 15.8%. RBI will face pressure to cut rates or relax CRR if deposit growth doesn't accelerate within 6-8 weeks. Watch for corporate bond issuance (₹134,000 cr / month) as alternative funding channel — this is the safety valve.","pct_10y":75,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 75th percentile historically preceded either RBI rate cuts or deposit mobilisation crises. Last time CD hit 82% was 2022 — followed by 6 months of NBFC stress and RBI liquidity injections.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadening Across Sectors","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (prev 16.1%), capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (prev 75.6%), both rising. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5% but still positive). Credit to industry at 19.5% YoY (19.2→20→18.2→19.5%, two of last three months up), agriculture credit at 19.5% YoY (16.8→17→17.2→19.5%, three months rising). Vehicle credit at 18.8% YoY (15.2→18.8→19.7→18.8%). Iron ore prices at $161.91/t, up sharply from $90.67/t prior month — signalling construction and steel demand.","implication":"Overweight capital goods manufacturers (Cummins, Escorts, Bharat Electronics) and cement (Ultratech, Ambuja) — capacity utilisation at 77.4% is the inflection point where new capex becomes rational. Domestic steel demand is real; iron ore spike is not speculative. Avoid housing credit plays (10.6% YoY, falling) — capex is infrastructure and industrial, not residential. Allocate to PSU banks with strong agri/industry lending books.","pct_10y":68,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle; historically, capex accelerates when CU crosses 75%. Last sustained capex upcycle (2014-2018) saw IIP capgoods average 12-14% — current 16.9% suggests front-loading ahead of potential policy tightening.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit 94th Percentile, Growth Slowing","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,160 cr / month (prev ₹32,490 cr / month), down 1% MoM but at 94th percentile of 10-year range. SIP YoY growth at 8.9% (down from 15% → 19.85% → 14% → 10.7% → 8.9%, five-month deceleration). MF AUM at ₹83.39 lakh cr (up from ₹82.64 lakh cr), at 86th percentile. Equity MF net inflows at ₹32,994 cr / month (down from ₹38,307 cr / month). SIP accounts at 10 mn (data anomaly: prev 1006 mn, likely reporting error; recent: 10.45→9.9→100.2→10.06→10 mn, volatile). This is late-cycle retail behaviour: affluent money entering, not mass retail expansion. Reduce overweight on small-cap and mid-cap funds; rotate to large-cap value and dividend-paying stocks. Expect SIP growth to stabilise at 5-7% YoY; not a growth driver anymore.","pct_10y":94,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 94th percentile but growth at 28th percentile — a classic late-cycle divergence. In 2021-2022, SIP inflows peaked at ₹35,000+ cr / month before a 18-month correction. Current plateau suggests retail saturation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens Margin Compression","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (prev 20.05%), up 288 bps in one month, at 95th percentile of 10-year range — highest in this cycle. WPI at 9.92% YoY (prev 9.78%), rising. Brent crude at $89.87/bbl (recent: 95.84→95.38→91.58→92.63→89.39→89.9, volatile but elevated). WTI at $83.62/bbl (recent: 88.56→88.31→85.01→85.06→82.35→82.79, downtrend). Natural gas at $3.791/MMBtu (recent: 3.23→3.15→3.09→3.18→3.37→3.24, volatile). FAO food index at 136 (prev 134.5), up 2 of last 3 months.","implication":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a red flag for RBI — expect CPI to remain sticky above 6% for 2-3 more months. This delays rate cuts and pressures corporate margins in logistics, cement, steel, and power. Avoid cyclicals with high fuel exposure (Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Dalmia Cement). Overweight defensive sectors: pharma, FMCG, IT services (low fuel intensity). Oil companies (ONGC, Reliance) benefit from higher crude, but refining margins compress. Hedge INR weakness — oil imports will widen CAD.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile last occurred in 2022 (pre-RBI tightening cycle). Sustained fuel inflation above 20% historically precedes 2-3 quarters of margin pressure and earnings downgrades in transport and manufacturing.","is_surprise":false}

signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Pullback","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (prev 2.81 mn sq ft / quarter), but recent data shows violent oscillation: 14.1→15.08→14.1→15.08→19.5→4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (last quarter crashed 79% from prior quarter). Office vacancy at 13.4% vacant (down from 14.5%), suggesting supply-side tightness, not demand strength. Rent in Bengaluru at ₹103.6/sqft/mo (recent: 109→163→103.6→168.8→168→103.6, highly volatile). Rent in Mumbai at ₹156/sqft/mo (recent: 178.7→156→135.8→342.6→343→156, equally volatile). Nifty IT at flat (recent: 25299→25144→25312→25387→25228→25514, no directional trend). US PMI composite at 58.4 (prev 56), rising 2 in a row (50.3→56→58.4) — US demand is strong. Nikkei 225 at 56,436.65 (falling 5 in a row: 61142→60519→58943→58697→59198→56990) — Japan weakness.","implication":"Office absorption collapse (4.02 mn sq ft, down 79% QoQ) is NOT a demand story — it's a GCC (Global Capability Centre) pullback. US demand is strong (PMI 58.4), but Indian IT services are not capturing it. This suggests: (1) GCCs are consolidating, not expanding; (2) automation is replacing headcount; (3) India's IT services are losing pricing power to automation vendors. Underweight TCS, Infosys, Wipro — their office real estate is a stranded asset. Overweight software-as-a-service (SaaS) and automation plays. The office vacancy decline (14.5% → 13.4%) is misleading — it's supply destruction, not demand recovery. Falsifiable: if GCC absorption rebounds to 15+ mn sq ft next quarter, this thesis is wrong.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft is a 10-year low (0th percentile). This is the first time absorption has crashed this hard while US PMI remains strong — a structural break suggesting GCC model is under stress, not cyclical weakness.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

Expansion on the Surface, Stress Beneath the Waterline

The facts:

  • GDP at 7.8% YoY with PMI Composite at 56.5 and IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY — three expansion signals in alignment.
  • But CPI at 6.09% YoY has breached the RBI's 6% ceiling for the first time this cycle, with core CPI accelerating to 4.5% YoY.
  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) feeds WPI at 9.92% YoY — margin compression is a quarter away from appearing in earnings.
  • FY full-year GDP estimate revised down to 7.1% YoY from 7.6% — the quarterly print flatters the annual trajectory.

The tension: Growth metrics signal broad expansion; inflation metrics signal the RBI's pause is becoming untenable. A real repo rate of negative 84 bps with CPI above the tolerance band is not a neutral policy stance — it is an inadvertent stimulus.

Bottom line: Watch November CPI: a third consecutive print above 6% forces the RBI's hand on the rate path regardless of growth optics.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Re-acceleration Meets BOJ Shock — EM Caught in the Crossfire

The facts:

  • US GDP SAAR at 3.4% SAAR (rising three consecutive quarters) with US PMI Composite at 58.4 — the US economy is not slowing.
  • But US CPI at 3.72% YoY (rising three months) and core PCE at 3.12% YoY mean the Fed at 3.88% p.a. is not done — US 10Y at 5.04% yield (91st percentile) is tightening for it.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. — a 100th-percentile print, up 25 bps — is unwinding the yen carry trade that funded EM allocations for a decade.
  • Euro Stoxx 50 at 5,942 (falling five consecutive sessions from 6,399) and Hang Seng at 22,411 (falling five in a row) confirm the risk-off is not US-specific.

The tension: US growth re-acceleration argues for higher-for-longer Fed rates; BOJ normalisation simultaneously withdraws the liquidity that made EM assets attractive at those rates. India faces both pressures simultaneously.

Bottom line: BOJ's next move is the underappreciated tail risk — a further 25 bps hike would accelerate yen carry unwind and trigger FII outflows India's DII base may not fully absorb.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Holds — But the Growth Engine Is Decelerating

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,160 cr / month (94th percentile) provide a structural floor — but YoY growth has decelerated five consecutive months to 8.9% YoY from a peak of 19.85% YoY.
  • Equity MF net inflows fell to ₹32,994 cr / month from ₹38,307 cr / month — a ₹5,313 cr / month drop in a single period.
  • FII equity net at -₹4,516 cr / month with DII equity net at ₹6,222 cr / month — domestic absorption is positive but narrowing.
  • But MF AUM at ₹83.39 lakh cr (86th percentile) masks the deceleration: the pool is large, but the marginal inflow is shrinking.

The tension: The SIP base is structurally sound; the flow momentum is not. Decelerating SIP growth alongside falling equity MF net inflows means the domestic liquidity cushion that absorbed FII selling in prior quarters is thinner than the AUM headline suggests.

Bottom line: If SIP YoY growth falls below 7%, the DII absorption capacity against a BOJ-driven FII exit becomes the critical test for Nifty support levels.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

REITs Pricing GCC Risk; Residential Bifurcating by City and Ticket

The facts:

  • NRI buying is FALLING — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (prior 15%, but down 2 pp vs earlier print); NRI share within premium/luxury at 32% — a pullback in the segment most sensitive to INR and global risk appetite.
  • Premium segment (₹80 lakh – ₹1.5 cr) is oversupplied at -3 pp (34% launch share vs 31% sales share); Hyderabad leads with 15% YoY sales growth but 28 months of unsold inventory.
  • Office absorption crashed to 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter — a 79% single-quarter drop — with GCCs at 42% of occupier mix most exposed to US tech spending decisions.
  • Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — all down 12–28% from prior prints, pricing the office absorption collapse correctly.

The tension: Residential demand in Bengaluru and Hyderabad is holding; office demand has fallen off a cliff. REITs are caught between strong physical vacancy metrics (Bengaluru office vacancy 13.4%) and a demand signal that contradicts them.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until GCC hiring data from US tech firms stabilises; in residential, Bengaluru premium (15-month inventory) is the only city with supply-demand balance.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Detonator — BOJ Lights the Match

The facts:

  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — yen carry unwind accelerates FII outflows from EM; India's FII equity net already at -₹4,516 cr / month.
  • CPI at 6.09% YoY above the RBI's 6% ceiling for the first time this cycle — forces a policy pivot that the market has not priced into the rate curve.
  • CD ratio at 82% (75th percentile) with services credit at 28.3% YoY (rising three months) — macro-prudential tightening via risk weights is the RBI's most likely next tool.
  • But S&P 500 at 6,910 (falling five consecutive sessions from 7,592) with US VIX at 35.89 (62nd percentile, rising four of last five) — a US equity correction amplifies all three risks simultaneously.

The tension: Each risk is manageable in isolation; the BOJ shock is the common factor that can trigger all three simultaneously — FII outflows stress the CD ratio, INR depreciation feeds CPI, and RBI is forced to tighten into a slowing global cycle.

Bottom line: Watch BOJ's next policy meeting: a further 25 bps hike above 1.25% p.a. is the single data point that converts three manageable risks into one cascading event.

"}
